question_text: The integral $\int_{0}^{1}\cot^{-1}(1+x+x^2)dx$ is equal to:
solution_text:
$I = \int_{0}^{1}\cot^{-1}(1+x+x^2)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{1+x+x^2}\right)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{(x+1)-x}{1+(x+1)x}\right)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}(\tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x)dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}(x+1)dx - \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}x dx$

Substituting $x+1 = t$ in the first integral:

$I = \int_{1}^{2}\tan^{-1}x dx - \int_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}x dx$

Using integration by parts, $\int \tan^{-1}x dx = x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)$

$I = \left[x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)\right]_{1}^{2} - \left[x\tan^{-1}x - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e(1+x^2)\right]_{0}^{1}$

$I = \left(2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2\right)\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2 - 0\right)$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 - \dfrac{\pi}{2} + \log_e 2$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 5 + \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 4 - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$I = 2\tan^{-1}2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right) - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $2\tan^{-1}2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log_e\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

question_text: If $\int\left(\frac{1-5 \cos ^{2} x}{\sin ^{5} x \cos ^{2} x}\right) d x=f(x)+\mathrm{C}$, where C is the constant of integration, then $f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ is equal to
solution_text:
$\int \frac{1 - 5\cos^2 x}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} dx = \int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x \cos^2 x} - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

$= \int \frac{\sec^2 x \, dx}{\sin^5 x} - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

By IBP:
$= \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} - \int \left(-\frac{5}{\sin^6 x}\right) \cos x \cdot \tan x \, dx - 5\int \frac{dx}{\sin^5 x}$

$= \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x} + C$

So $f(x) = \frac{\tan x}{\sin^5 x}$

$f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) - f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{2^5}{\sqrt{3}} - (\sqrt{2})^5 = \frac{32}{\sqrt{3}} - 4\sqrt{2} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}(8 - \sqrt{6})$

question_text: Let $\mathrm{f}: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f(2)=1$. If $\mathrm{F}(x)=x f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbf{R}$, $\int_0^2 x \mathrm{~F}^{\prime}(x) \mathrm{d} x=6$ and $\int_0^2 x^2 \mathrm{~F}^{\prime \prime}(x) \mathrm{d} x=40$, then $\mathrm{F}^{\prime}(2)+\int_0^2 \mathrm{~F}(x) \mathrm{d} x$ is equal to :
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}
& \int_0^2 \mathrm{xF}^{\prime}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=6 \\
& =\left.\mathrm{xF}(\mathrm{x})\right|_0 ^2-\int_0^2 \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=6 \\
& =2 \mathrm{~F}(2)-\int_0^2 \mathrm{xF}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=6[\therefore \mathrm{f}(2)=2 \mathrm{~F}(2)=2] \\
& \int_0^2 \mathrm{xF}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=-2 ...(1)\\
& \Rightarrow \int_0^2 \mathrm{~F}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=-2 ...(2)
\end{aligned}$

Also
$\int_0^2 x^2 F^{\prime \prime}(x) d x=\left.x^2 F^{\prime}(x)\right|_0 ^2-2 \int_0^2 x^{\prime} F^{\prime}(x) d x=40$
$\begin{aligned} & =4 F^{\prime}(2)-2 \times 6=40 \\ & F^{\prime}(2)=13 \\ & \therefore F^{\prime}(2)+\int_0^2 F(x)=13-2=11\end{aligned}$

The integral $\int_{7 \pi / 4}^{7 \pi / 3} \sqrt{\tan ^2 x} d x$ is equal to :

Let $\mathrm{I}=\int_{7 \pi / 4}^{7 \pi / 3} \sqrt{\tan ^2 x} d x$
$$
=\int_{7 \pi / 4}^{7 \pi / 3} \tan x d x=-\left.\log \cos x\right|_{7 \pi / 4} ^{7 \pi / 3}
$$
$=-\left[\log \cos \frac{7 \pi}{3}-\log \cos \frac{7 \pi}{4}\right]$
$=\log \cos \frac{7 \pi}{4}-\log \cos \frac{7 \pi}{3}$

question_text: The value of $k \in \mathrm{N}$ for which the integral $I_n=\int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^n d x, n \in \mathbb{N}$, satisfies $147 I_{20}=148 I_{21}$ is
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & I_n=\int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^n \cdot 1 d x \\ & I_n=\left(1-x^k\right)^n \cdot x-n k \int_0^1\left(1-x^k\right)^{n-1} \cdot x^{k-1} \cdot d x \\ & I_n=n k \int_0^1\left[\left(1-x^k\right)^n-\left(1-x^k\right)^{n-1}\right] d x \\ & I_n=n k I_n-n k I_n \\ & \frac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}=\frac{n k}{n k+1} \\ & \frac{I_{21}}{I_{20}}=\frac{21 k}{1+21 k} \\ & =\frac{147}{148} \Rightarrow k=7\end{aligned}$

question_text: If $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\left(\cot\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\cot\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+1\right)dx = \alpha\log_e(\sqrt{3}-1)$, then $9\alpha^2$ is equal to ________.
solution_text:
Given integral is $I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\left(\cot\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\cot\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+1\right)dx$

Using the identity $\cot A \cot B + 1 = \dfrac{\cos(A-B)}{\sin A \sin B}$, the integrand simplifies to:

$f(x) = \dfrac{\cos\left(\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)}{\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}$

$f(x) = \dfrac{\cos\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)}{\sin^2 x - \sin^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}$

$f(x) = \dfrac{-1/2}{\sin^2 x - 3/4} = \dfrac{2}{3 - 4\sin^2 x}$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $\cos^2 x$:

$f(x) = \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3\sec^2 x - 4\tan^2 x} = \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3(1+\tan^2 x) - 4\tan^2 x} = \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3 - \tan^2 x}$

The integral becomes:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{2\sec^2 x}{3 - \tan^2 x} dx$

Substituting $\tan x = t \Rightarrow \sec^2 x dx = dt$.

When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $t = 1$.

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{1} \dfrac{2}{3 - t^2} dt$

Using the standard integral $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{a^2 - x^2} dx = \dfrac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\dfrac{a+x}{a-x}\right|$:

$I = 2 \left[ \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \ln\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+t}{\sqrt{3}-t}\right| \right]_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{1}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}\right) - \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\right) \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}\right) - \ln\left(\dfrac{3+1}{3-1}\right) \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}\right) - \ln 2 \right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)}\right)$

Rationalizing the term inside the logarithm by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by $(\sqrt{3}-1)$:

$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{3}+1)(\sqrt{3}-1)}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)^2} = \dfrac{3-1}{2(\sqrt{3}-1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{(\sqrt{3}-1)^2} = (\sqrt{3}-1)^{-2}$

Thus,

$I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \ln\left((\sqrt{3}-1)^{-2}\right) = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \ln(\sqrt{3}-1)$

Comparing this with $I = \alpha\log_e(\sqrt{3}-1)$, we get:

$\alpha = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

Therefore, $9\alpha^2 = 9 \left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = 9 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 12$.

Answer: $12$

question_text: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x(x^2+x+1)}}{(\sqrt{x+1})(\sqrt{x^4+x^2+1})} \, dx$ is equal to:
solution_text:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x(x^2 + x + 1)}}{\sqrt{x + 1}\,\sqrt{x^4 + x^2 + 1}}\, dx$.

Using the identity $x^4 + x^2 + 1 = (x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1)$:
$I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}\,\sqrt{x^2 + x + 1}}{\sqrt{x + 1}\,\sqrt{(x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1)}}\, dx$

Cancelling $\sqrt{x^2 + x + 1}$:
$I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{(x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1)}}\, dx$

Using $(x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1) = x^3 + 1$:
$I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^3 + 1}}\, dx$

Substitution:
Let $t = x^{3/2}$, so $dt = \dfrac{3}{2}x^{1/2}\, dx \Rightarrow \sqrt{x}\, dx = \dfrac{2}{3}\, dt$.

Also, $t^2 = x^3$, so $x^3 + 1 = t^2 + 1$.

Changing limits:
$x = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0$
$x = 2 \Rightarrow t = 2^{3/2} = 2\sqrt{2}$

Therefore:
$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2 + 1}}$

Using $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2 + a^2}} = \log_e\left|t + \sqrt{t^2 + a^2}\right| + C$:
$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\left[\log_e\left(t + \sqrt{t^2 + 1}\right)\right]_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}}$

$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\left[\log_e\left(2\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{8 + 1}\right) - \log_e(1)\right]$

$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\log_e\left(2\sqrt{2} + 3\right)$

$I = \dfrac{2}{3}\log_e\left(3 + 2\sqrt{2}\right)$

Hence, the correct option is $(3)\ \dfrac{2}{3}\log_e\left(3 + 2\sqrt{2}\right)$.

question_text: Let $(2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a})$, $f(a)$, $(3^a + 3^{-a})$ be in A.P. and $\alpha$ be the minimum value of $f(a)$. Then the value of the integral $\int_{\log_e(\alpha-1)}^{\log_e(\alpha)} \dfrac{dx}{(e^{2x} - e^{-2x})}$ is :
solution_text:
Since $(2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a})$, $f(a)$, and $(3^a + 3^{-a})$ are in A.P., we have:

$2f(a) = 2^{1-a} + 2^{1+a} + 3^a + 3^{-a}$

$f(a) = (2^{-a} + 2^a) + \dfrac{1}{2}(3^a + 3^{-a})$

Using the AM-GM inequality, $x + \dfrac{1}{x} \ge 2$ for $x > 0$.

$2^a + 2^{-a} \ge 2$ and $3^a + 3^{-a} \ge 2$.

The minimum value of $f(a)$ occurs when $a = 0$.

$\alpha = f(0) = (2^0 + 2^0) + \dfrac{1}{2}(3^0 + 3^0) = 2 + 1 = 3$.

Now, we evaluate the integral:

$I = \int_{\log_e 2}^{\log_e 3} \dfrac{dx}{e^{2x} - e^{-2x}} = \int_{\log_e 2}^{\log_e 3} \dfrac{e^{2x}}{e^{4x} - 1} dx$

Let $e^{2x} = t \Rightarrow 2e^{2x} dx = dt$.

When $x = \log_e 2$, $t = e^{2\log_e 2} = 4$.

When $x = \log_e 3$, $t = e^{2\log_e 3} = 9$.

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{4}^{9} \dfrac{dt}{t^2 - 1}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e \left| \dfrac{t-1}{t+1} \right| \right]_{4}^{9}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \log_e \dfrac{8}{10} - \log_e \dfrac{3}{5} \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \log_e \dfrac{4}{5} - \log_e \dfrac{3}{5} \right) = \dfrac{1}{4} \log_e \left( \dfrac{4/5}{3/5} \right) = \dfrac{1}{4} \log_e \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4} \log_e\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$

question_text: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(\dfrac{4 - \csc^2 x}{\cos^4 x}\right) dx$ is:
solution_text:
The given integral is $I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(\dfrac{4 - \csc^2 x}{\cos^4 x}\right) dx$.

We can rewrite the integrand in terms of $\tan x$ and $\sec x$. Using the identity $\csc^2 x = 1 + \cot^2 x = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 x}$, we get:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(4 - 1 - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 x}\right) \sec^4 x \, dx$

$I = \displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(3 - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 x}\right) (1 + \tan^2 x) \sec^2 x \, dx$

Substitute $t = \tan x$, which gives $dt = \sec^2 x \, dx$.

The limits of integration change as follows:
When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $t = \sqrt{3}$.

The integral becomes:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(3 - \dfrac{1}{t^2}\right) (1 + t^2) dt$

Expanding the integrand, we get:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(3 + 3t^2 - \dfrac{1}{t^2} - 1\right) dt$

$I = \displaystyle\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(3t^2 + 2 - t^{-2}\right) dt$

Integrating with respect to $t$:

$I = \left[ t^3 + 2t + \dfrac{1}{t} \right]_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}$

Substitute the upper limit $t = \sqrt{3}$:

$\left( \sqrt{3} \right)^3 + 2\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 3\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{48}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Substitute the lower limit $t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$:

$\left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)^3 + 2\left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) + \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}} + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} + \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1 + 6 + 9}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Subtracting the lower limit value from the upper limit value:

$I = \dfrac{48}{3\sqrt{3}} - \dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{32}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{32}{3\sqrt{3}}$

question_text: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \dfrac{\log_e(x)}{x^2 + 4}\,dx$ is:
solution_text:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_0^\infty \dfrac{\log_e(x)}{x^2 + 4}\,dx$

Substitute $x = 2 \tan \theta$, which gives $dx = 2 \sec^2 \theta \,d\theta$.

The limits of integration change from $x = 0 \to \theta = 0$ to $x \to \infty \to \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\log_e(2 \tan \theta)}{4 \tan^2 \theta + 4} (2 \sec^2 \theta) \,d\theta$

$I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\log_e(2 \tan \theta)}{4 \sec^2 \theta} (2 \sec^2 \theta) \,d\theta$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(2 \tan \theta) \,d\theta$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} (\log_e 2 + \log_e(\tan \theta)) \,d\theta$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e 2 \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} 1 \,d\theta + \dfrac{1}{2} \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\tan \theta) \,d\theta$

Let $I_1 = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\tan \theta) \,d\theta$

Using the property $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \displaystyle\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx$, we get:

$I_1 = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e\left(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\right) \,d\theta = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\cot \theta) \,d\theta$

$I_1 = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan \theta}\right) \,d\theta = -\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log_e(\tan \theta) \,d\theta = -I_1$

$2I_1 = 0 \Rightarrow I_1 = 0$

Substituting $I_1 = 0$ back into the equation for $I$:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e 2 \left[\theta\right]_0^{\pi/2} + 0$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \log_e 2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi \log_e 2}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi\log_e(2)}{4}$

question_text: If $\int_{0}^{1} 4 \cot ^{-1}\left(1-2 x+4 x^{2}\right) \mathrm{d} x=\mathrm{atan}^{-1}(2)-\mathrm{blog}_{\mathrm{e}}(5)$, where $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b} \in \mathbf{N}$, then $(2 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
solution_text:
Let $I=\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}\left(1-2 x+4 x^2\right) d x$
$I=\int_0^1\left(\cot ^{-1}(2 x-1)-\cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x$

Applying king
$I=\int_0^1\left(-\cot ^{-1}(2 x-1)+\cot ^{-1}(2 x-2)\right) d x$

From (1) and (2)

$2 I=\int_0^1\left(\cot ^{-1}(2 x-2)-\cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x$
$=\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x-2) d x-\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x) d x$

Applying King

$=\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(-2 x) d x-\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x) d x$
$=\int_0^1\left(\pi-\cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x-\int_0^1 \cot ^{-1}(2 x) d x$
$=\int_0^1\left(\pi-2 \cot ^{-1}(2 x)\right) d x$
$=\pi-2 \int_0^1\left(\cot ^{-1} 2 x\right) \cdot 1 d x$

By parts
$=\pi-2\left[\left(x \cot ^{-1} 2 x\right)_0^1+\int_0^1 \frac{2 x}{1+4 x^2} d x\right]$

Let $1+4 \mathrm{x}^2=\mathrm{t}$
$8 \mathrm{xdx}=\mathrm{dt}$
$=\pi-2\left[\cot ^{-1} 2+\frac{1}{4} \int_1^5 \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{t}}\right]$
$=\pi-2 \cot ^{-1} 2-\frac{1}{2} \ell \mathrm{n} 5$
$2 \mathrm{I}=2 \tan ^{-1} 2-\frac{1}{2} \ell \mathrm{n} 5$
$\Rightarrow 4 \mathrm{I}=4 \tan ^{-1} 2-\ell \mathrm{n} 5$
$\therefore 2 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}=8+1=9$

question_text: The integral \(80 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\frac{\sin \theta+\cos \theta}{9+16 \sin 2 \theta}\right) d \theta\) is equal to :
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\frac{\sin \theta+\cos \theta}{9-16 \sin 2 \theta}\right) d \theta \\ & \text { Take } \sin \theta-\cos \theta=t \\ & (\cos \theta+\sin \theta) d \theta=d t \\ & (\sin \theta-\cos \theta)^2=t^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \sin 2 \theta=1-t^2 \\ & \theta=0 \rightarrow t=-1 \\ & \quad \theta=\frac{\pi}{4} \rightarrow t=0 \\ & I=\int_{-1}^0 \frac{d t}{9+16\left(1-t^2\right)} \\ & =\frac{1}{16} \int_{-1}^0 \frac{d t}{25} \frac{16}{16}-t^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{1}{10} \log _{\left\lvert\, \frac{5+4 t}{}\right.}^{5-4 t}\right]_{-1}^0 \\ & =\frac{1}{40}\left[0+\log _e 9\right] \\ & I=\frac{\log _e 9}{40} \\ & 80 I=2 \log _e 9 \\ & 80 I=4 \log _e 3\end{aligned}$

question_text: Let for $f(x)=7 \tan ^8 x+7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^4 x-3 \tan ^2 x, \quad \mathrm{I}_1=\int_0^{\pi / 4} f(x) \mathrm{d} x$ and $\mathrm{I}_2=\int_0^{\pi / 4} x f(x) \mathrm{d} x$. Then $7 \mathrm{I}_1+12 \mathrm{I}_2$ is equal to :
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned} f(x) & =7 \tan ^8 x+7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^4 x-3 \tan ^2 x \\ & =7 \tan ^6 x\left(1+\tan ^2 x\right)-3 \tan ^2 x\left(1+\tan ^2 x\right) \\ & =\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right)\left(1+\tan ^2 x\right) \\ & =\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right) \sec ^2 x \\ l_1= & \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} f(x) d x=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right) \sec ^2 x d x \\ & =\left.\left(\frac{7 \tan ^7 x}{7}-\frac{3 \tan ^3 x}{3}\right)\right|_0 ^{\frac{\pi}{4}}=1-1=0\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}
I_2= & \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x f(x) d x=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x\left(7 \tan ^6 x-3 \tan ^2 x\right) \sec ^2 x d x \\
& =\left.x\left(\tan ^7 x-\tan ^3 x\right)\right|_0 ^{\frac{\pi}{4}}-\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} 1 \cdot\left(\tan ^7 x-\tan ^3 x\right) d x \\
& =0-\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan ^3 x\left(\tan ^2 x-1\right)\left(\tan ^2 x+1\right) d x \\
& =\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\tan ^3 x-\tan ^5 x\right) \sec ^2 x d x=\frac{\tan ^4 x}{4}-\left.\frac{\tan ^6 x}{6}\right|_0 ^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\
& =\frac{1}{12}
\end{aligned}$

Hence $7 I_1+12 I_2=1$

question_text: Let $\int_\alpha^{\log _e 4} \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\sqrt{\mathrm{e}^x-1}}=\frac{\pi}{6}$. Then $\mathrm{e}^\alpha$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha}$ are the roots of the equation :
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & \int_\alpha^{\log 4} \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}-1}}=\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & \text { Let } \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}-1=\mathrm{t}^2 \\ & \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{dx}=2 \mathrm{t} \mathrm{dt} \\ & =\int \frac{2 \mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{t}^2+1} \\ & =2 \tan ^{-1} \mathrm{t} \\ & =\left.2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}-1}\right)\right|_\alpha ^{\log _{\mathrm{e}}^4} \\ & =2\left[\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{3}-\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1}\right]=\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{3}-\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1}=\frac{\pi}{12} \\ & \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} \sqrt{\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ & \mathrm{e}^\alpha=2 \quad \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha}=\frac{1}{2} \\ & \mathrm{x}^2-\left(2+\frac{1}{2}\right) \mathrm{x}+1=0 \\ & 2 \mathrm{x}^2-5 \mathrm{x}+2=0\end{aligned}$

question_text: If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><mn>15</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msqrt><msup><mfenced><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mn>3</mn></msup></msqrt></msqrt></mfrac><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></math> are integers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi></math> is equal to

question_text: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi></math> be a differentiable function satisfying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mfenced><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></mfrac><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mfenced><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mi>d</mi><mi>λ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mfenced><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>. fx=23∫03fλ2x3dλ

So, fx=3x

So fα=6⇒36=3α

question_text: The value of integral $\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}} \frac{x}{1+\sin x} d x$ is
solution_text:
Let $I=\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}} \frac{x}{1+\sin x} d x$ also let $K=\frac{x}{1+\sin x}$
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $(1-\sin x)$, we get;
$$
\begin{aligned}
K &=\frac{x(1-\sin x)}{1-(\sin x)^2}=\frac{x(1-\sin x)}{(\cos x)^2} \\
&=x(1-\sin x) \sec ^2 x \\
&=x \sec ^2 x-x \sin x \sec ^2 x=x \sec ^2 x-x \tan \\
x & \sec x
\end{aligned}
$$
Now, $I=\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}} x \sec ^2 x d x-\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}} x \sec x \tan x d x$
$$
=\left[x \tan x-\int \frac{d x}{d x} \tan x d x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}}-\left[x \sec x-\int \frac{d x}{d x} \sec x d x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&=[x \tan x-\ln |\sec x|]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}} \\
&-[x \sec x-\ln |\sec x+\tan x|]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{4}}+c \\
&\Rightarrow I=\left\{\left[\frac{3 \pi}{4} \tan \frac{3 \pi}{4}-\ln \left|\frac{3 \pi}{4}\right|\right.\right. \\
&\left.-\left[\frac{3 \pi}{4} \sec \frac{3 \pi}{4}-\ln \left|\sec \frac{3 \pi}{4}+\tan \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right|\right]\right\} \\

question_text: If for $\mathrm{n} \geq 1, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{n}}=\int_1^{\mathrm{e}}\left(\log \mathrm{x}^{\mathrm{n}}\right) \mathrm{dx}$, then $\mathrm{P}_{10}-90 \mathrm{P}_8$ is equal to:

Also, when $x=1$, then $t=\log 1=0$ and when $x=e$, then $t=\log _e e=1$
$$
\begin{gathered}
\therefore \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{n}}=\int_0^1 t^n \cdot e^t d t \\
\therefore \mathrm{P}_{10}=\int_0^1 t^{10} e^t d t \text { and } \mathrm{P}_8=\int_0^1 t^8 e^t d t \\
\text { Now, } \mathrm{P}_{10}-90 \mathrm{P}_8=\int_0^1 t^{10} e^t d t-90 \int_0^1 t^8 e^t d t \\
\mathrm{P}_{10}-90 \mathrm{P}_8 \\
\mathrm{P}_{10}-90 \mathrm{P}_8 \\
=\left[t^{10} e^t\right]_0^1-10 \int_0^1 t^9 e^t d t-90 \int_0^1 t^8 e^t d t \\
\mathrm{P}_{10}-90 \mathrm{P}_8= \\
e-10\left[t^9 \int_0^1 e^t d t-\int_0^1 \frac{d}{d t}\left(t^9\right) \int e^t d t\right]-90 \int_0^1 t^8 e^t d t
\end{gathered}
$$

$$
\begin{gathered}

question_text:
For $0 \leq x \leq \frac{\pi}{2}$, the value of
$$
\int_0^{\sin ^2 x} \sin ^{-1}(\sqrt{t}) d t+\int_0^{\cos ^2 x} \cos ^{-1}(\sqrt{t}) d t \text { equals : }
$$
solution_text:
Consider
$$
\int_0^{\sin ^2 x} \sin ^{-1}(\sqrt{t}) d t+\int_0^{\cos ^2 x} \cos ^{-1}(\sqrt{t}) d t
$$
Let $\mathrm{I}=f(x)$ after integrating and putting the limits.
$$
\begin{aligned}
&f^{\prime}(x)=\sin ^{-1} \sqrt{\sin ^2 x}(2 \sin x \cos x)-0 \\
&\quad+\cos ^{-1} \sqrt{\cos ^2 x}(-2 \cos x \sin x)-0 \\
&\therefore f^{\prime}(x)=0 \Rightarrow f(x)=\mathrm{C} \quad \text { (constant) }
\end{aligned}
$$
Now, we find $f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \mathrm{I} &=\int_0^{1 / 2} \sin ^{-1} \sqrt{t} d t+\int_0^{1 / 2} \cos ^{-1} \sqrt{t} d t \\
&=\int_0^{1 / 2}\left(\sin ^{-1} \sqrt{t}+\cos ^{-1} \sqrt{t}\right) d t \\
&=\int_0^{1 / 2} \frac{\pi}{2} d t=\frac{\pi}{4}=\mathrm{C} \\
\therefore \quad f(x)=\frac{\pi}{4} \\
\therefore \text { Required integration }=\frac{\pi}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

question_text:
Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be such that $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$, for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f(0) \neq 0$. Let $g: [1, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that
$x^2 g(x) = \int\limits_1^x (t^2 f(t) - tg(t))\,dt$.
Then $g(2)$ is equal to :
solution_text:
Given $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f(0) \neq 0$.

Substituting $y = 0$, we get $f(0) = f(x)f(0)$.

Since $f(0) \neq 0$, dividing by $f(0)$ gives $f(x) = 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

The given integral equation is:

$x^2 g(x) = \int\limits_1^x (t^2 f(t) - tg(t))\,dt$

Substituting $f(t) = 1$:

$x^2 g(x) = \int\limits_1^x (t^2 - tg(t))\,dt$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ using Leibniz's rule:

$2x g(x) + x^2 g'(x) = x^2 - xg(x)$

$x^2 g'(x) + 3xg(x) = x^2$

Dividing by $x$ (since $x \ge 1$):

$x g'(x) + 3g(x) = x$

$g'(x) + \dfrac{3}{x}g(x) = 1$

This is a linear differential equation. The integrating factor is:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int \dfrac{3}{x}\,dx} = e^{3\ln x} = x^3$

Multiplying the differential equation by $x^3$:

$x^3 g'(x) + 3x^2 g(x) = x^3$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3 g(x)) = x^3$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$x^3 g(x) = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + C$

From the integral equation, substituting $x = 1$ gives $1^2 g(1) = \int\limits_1^1 (t^2 - tg(t))\,dt = 0$, so $g(1) = 0$.

Substituting $x = 1$ and $g(1) = 0$ into the integrated equation:

$1^3(0) = \dfrac{1^4}{4} + C \Rightarrow C = -\dfrac{1}{4}$

Thus, the function $g(x)$ is given by:

$x^3 g(x) = \dfrac{x^4 - 1}{4}$

$g(x) = \dfrac{x^4 - 1}{4x^3}$

Substituting $x = 2$:

$g(2) = \dfrac{2^4 - 1}{4(2^3)} = \dfrac{16 - 1}{32} = \dfrac{15}{32}$

Answer: $\dfrac{15}{32}$

question_text: Let $f: [1, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ be a differentiable function defined as $f(x) = \int_1^x f(t)\,dt + (1-x)(\log_e x - 1) + e$. Then the value of $f(f(1))$ is :
solution_text:
Given $f(x) = \int_1^x f(t)\,dt + (1-x)(\log_e x - 1) + e$

Substituting $x = 1$ in the given equation:

$f(1) = \int_1^1 f(t)\,dt + (1-1)(\log_e 1 - 1) + e$

$f(1) = 0 + 0 + e = e$

Differentiating the given equation with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz rule:

$f'(x) = f(x) + \dfrac{d}{dx}[(1-x)(\log_e x - 1)]$

$f'(x) = f(x) + (-1)(\log_e x - 1) + (1-x)\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$

$f'(x) = f(x) - \log_e x + 1 + \dfrac{1}{x} - 1$

$f'(x) - f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x} - \log_e x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$, where $P = -1$ and $Q = \dfrac{1}{x} - \log_e x$.

Integrating Factor (IF) $= e^{\int -1 \,dx} = e^{-x}$

Multiplying the differential equation by the IF:

$e^{-x} f'(x) - e^{-x} f(x) = e^{-x} \left(\dfrac{1}{x} - \log_e x\right)$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} f(x)] = e^{-x} \dfrac{1}{x} - e^{-x} \log_e x$

Notice that $\dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} \log_e x] = -e^{-x} \log_e x + e^{-x} \dfrac{1}{x}$.

Thus, $\dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} f(x)] = \dfrac{d}{dx}[e^{-x} \log_e x]$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$e^{-x} f(x) = e^{-x} \log_e x + C$

$f(x) = \log_e x + C e^x$

Using the initial condition $f(1) = e$:

$e = \log_e 1 + C e^1$

$e = 0 + C e \Rightarrow C = 1$

Therefore, the function is $f(x) = \log_e x + e^x$.

We need to find $f(f(1))$:

Since $f(1) = e$, we evaluate $f(e)$:

$f(e) = \log_e e + e^e = 1 + e^e$

Answer: $(1 + e^e)$

question_text: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\tan(t-x)dt-\int_{0}^{x}f(t)\tan t\,dt$, $x \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Then $f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+12f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is equal to ______
solution_text:
Given the function:

$f(x) = \int_{0}^{x} \tan(t-x) dt - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$

First, we simplify the first integral. Let $u = x - t$, then $du = -dt$. When $t = 0$, $u = x$; when $t = x$, $u = 0$.

$\int_{0}^{x} \tan(t-x) dt = \int_{x}^{0} \tan(-u) (-du) = \int_{x}^{0} \tan u \, du = -\int_{0}^{x} \tan u \, du = -[\ln(\sec u)]_{0}^{x} = -\ln(\sec x) = \ln(\cos x)$

So, the equation becomes:

$f(x) = \ln(\cos x) - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz rule:

$f'(x) = \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x} - f(x) \tan x$

$f'(x) + f(x) \tan x = -\tan x$

This is a linear first-order differential equation. The integrating factor (IF) is:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int \tan x \, dx} = e^{\ln(\sec x)} = \sec x$

Multiplying the differential equation by $\sec x$:

$f'(x) \sec x + f(x) \sec x \tan x = -\sec x \tan x$

$\dfrac{d}{dx} (f(x) \sec x) = -\sec x \tan x$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$f(x) \sec x = -\sec x + C$

To find $C$, we use the initial condition. From $f(x) = \ln(\cos x) - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$, substituting $x = 0$ gives $f(0) = \ln(1) - 0 = 0$.

$0 \cdot \sec 0 = -\sec 0 + C \Rightarrow 0 = -1 + C \Rightarrow C = 1$

Thus, $f(x) \sec x = 1 - \sec x$

$f(x) = \cos x - 1$

Now, we find the required derivatives:

$f'(x) = -\sin x$

$f''(x) = -\cos x$

Evaluating these at the given points:

$f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - 1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1$

$f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Finally, substituting these values into the required expression:

$f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + 12f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 12\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1\right)$

$= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 6 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1 = 5$

Answer: $5$

question_text: If $f(x)$ satisfies the relation $f(x)=e^{x}+\int_{0}^{1}\left(y+x e^{x}\right) f(y) d y$, then $e+f(0)$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
solution_text:
$f(x) = e^x + \displaystyle\int_0^1 (y + xe^x)f(y)\, dy$

Splitting the integral:
$f(x) = e^x + \displaystyle\int_0^1 yf(y)\, dy + xe^x \int_0^1 f(y)\, dy$

Let $A = \displaystyle\int_0^1 yf(y)\, dy$ and $B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 f(y)\, dy$

$\Rightarrow f(x) = (1 + Bx)e^x + A$

At $x = 0$: $f(0) = 1 + A$

Now compute $B$ using the expression for $f(y)$:
$B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 \left[(1 + By)e^y + A\right] dy$
$B = \displaystyle\int_0^1 e^y\, dy + B\int_0^1 ye^y\, dy + \int_0^1 A\, dy$

Evaluating each integral:
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^y\, dy = e - 1$
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 ye^y\, dy = [ye^y]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^y\, dy = e - (e - 1) = 1$
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 A\, dy = A$

$\Rightarrow B = (e - 1) + B(1) + A$
$\Rightarrow 0 = e - 1 + A$
$\Rightarrow A = 1 - e$

$f(0) = 1 + A = 1 + (1 - e) = 2 - e$

$e + f(0) = e + (2 - e) = 2$

Answer: $2$

question_text: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy the equation $\int_{0}^{36} f\left(\frac{t x}{36}\right) d t=4 \alpha f(x)$. If $y=f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through the points $(2,1)$ and $(-4, \beta)$, then $\beta^{\alpha}$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
solution_text:
From $\int_0^{36} f\left(\frac{tx}{36}\right) dt = 4\alpha f(x)$, substitute $u = \frac{tx}{36}$ to get $\frac{36}{x} \int_0^x f(u) du = 4\alpha f(x)$.
Differentiating: $f(x) = \frac{\alpha}{9}[f(x) + xf'(x)]$, which simplifies to $(9-\alpha)f(x) = \alpha x f'(x)$.
This gives $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} = \frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha x}$, integrating to $f(x) = Kx^{\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha}}$.
For f to be a standard parabola: $\frac{9-\alpha}{\alpha} = 2 \Rightarrow \alpha = 3$.
Thus $f(x) = Kx^2$. Using point $(2,1)$: $K = \frac{1}{4}$, so $f(x) = \frac{x^2}{4}$.
At $(-4, \beta)$: $\beta = \frac{16}{4} = 4$.
Therefore $\beta^\alpha = 4^3 = 64$

question_text:
The number of elements in the
set $\mathrm{S}=\left\{x: x \in[0,100]\right.$ and $\left.\int_{0}^{x} t^{2} \sin (x-t) \mathrm{d} t=x^{2}\right\}$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
solution_text:
Using $u = x - t$: $\int_0^x t^2 \sin(x-t)\,dt = \int_0^x (x-u)^2 \sin u\,du$.
Expanding and integrating term by term:
$= x^2(1-\cos x) - 2x(-x\cos x + \sin x) + (-x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x - 2)$
$= x^2 + 2\cos x - 2$.
Setting equal to $x^2$: $2\cos x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow \cos x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 2n\pi$.
In $[0, 100]$: $2n\pi \le 100 \Rightarrow n \le \frac{50}{\pi} \approx 15.9$.
So $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 15$, giving $16$ elements.

question_text: Let $f(x)=\int_0^t t\left(t^2-9 t+20\right) d t, 1 \leq x \leq 5$. If the range of $f$ is $[\alpha, \beta]$, then $4(\alpha+\beta)$ equals :
solution_text:
$f^{\prime}(x)=x\left(x^2-9 x+20\right), x \in(1,5)$ $=(x-4) x(x-5)$
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)>0 \forall x \in(1,4) \\ & \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x) < 0 \forall x \in(4,5) \\ & \Rightarrow f(x) \text { increasing in }(1,4) \\ & \quad f(x) \text { decreasing in }(4,5) \\ & \Rightarrow \text { critical points to check: }\end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & x=1,4,5 \\ & f(x)=\int_0^x\left(t^3-9 t^2+20 t\right) d t \\ & =\frac{t^4}{4}-3 t^3+\left.10 t^2\right|_0 ^x=\frac{x^4}{4}-3 x^3+10 x^2 \\ & f(1)=\frac{1}{4}-3+10=\frac{29}{4} \\ & f(4)=4^3-3.4^3+10.4^2=-2.4^3+10.4^2=32 \\ & f(5)=\frac{5^4}{4}-3.5^3+10.25=\frac{5^4}{4}-125=\frac{125}{4}\end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text { Range } \Rightarrow\left[\frac{29}{4}, 32\right] \Rightarrow 4(\alpha+\beta)=128+29 \\ & =157\end{aligned}$

question_text: Let \(f:(0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbf{R}\) be a twice differentiable function. If for some \(\mathrm{a} \neq 0, \int_0^1 f(\lambda x) \mathrm{d} \lambda=\mathrm{a} f(x), f(1)=1\) and \(f(16)=\frac{1}{8}\), then \(16-f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)\) is equal to _______.
solution_text:
Given, $\int_0^1 f(\lambda x) d \lambda=a f(x)$
Let $\lambda x=u$
$d \lambda=\frac{1}{x} d u$
$\therefore$ From (1) $\frac{1}{x} \int_0^x f(u) d u=a f(x)$
$\Rightarrow \int_0^x f(u) d u=\operatorname{axf}(x)$
Differentiate both sides
$\begin{aligned}
& f(x)=a\left(x f^{\prime}(x)+f(x)\right) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f(x)=a x f^{\prime}(x)+a f(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(1-a) f(x)=a x f^{\prime}(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{(1-a)}{a} \cdot \frac{1}{x}
\end{aligned}$
Integrate both side w.r.t. ( $x$ )
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \int \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} d x=\frac{(1-a)}{a} \int \frac{1}{x} d x \\
& \Rightarrow \ln f(x)=\left(\frac{1-a}{a}\right) \ln x+c
\end{aligned}$
Now at $x=1 f(1)=1$
$\Rightarrow c=0$
Also given $f(16)=\frac{1}{8}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \frac{1}{8}=(16)^{\frac{1-a}{a}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2^{-3}=2^{\frac{4-4 a}{a}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-3=\frac{4-4 a}{a} \\
& \Rightarrow-3 a=4-4 a \\
& \Rightarrow a=4 \\
& \therefore \quad f(x)=x^{-3 / 4} \\
& f(x)=\frac{-3}{4} x^{-\frac{7}{4}}
\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & \text { Put } x=\frac{1}{16} \\ & f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)=\frac{-3}{4}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)^{-7 / 4}=\frac{-3}{4} \cdot 2^{-4 x\left(\frac{-7}{4}\right)}=-96 \\ & \therefore \quad 16-f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) \Rightarrow 16-(-96)=112\end{aligned}$

question_text: Let $f$ be a real valued continuous function defined on the positive real axis such that $g(x)=\int_0^x \mathrm{t} f(\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{dt}$. If $\mathrm{g}\left(x^3\right)=x^6+x^7$, then value of $\sum_{r=1}^{15} f\left(\mathrm{r}^3\right)$ is :
solution_text:
$g(x)=x^2+x^{7 / 3}$
$\begin{aligned} & g^{\prime}(x)=2 x+\frac{7}{3} x^{4 / 3} \\ & f(x)=\frac{g^{\prime}(x)}{x} \\ & f(x)=2+\frac{7}{3} x^{1 / 3} \\ & f\left(r^3\right)=2+\frac{7}{3} r \\ & \sum_{r=1}^{15}\left(2+\frac{7}{3} r\right)=2(15)+\frac{7}{3}\left(\frac{15(16)}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$
$=310$

question_text: Let for some function $\mathrm{y}=f(x), \int_0^x t f(t) d t=x^2 f(x), x\gt0$ and $f(2)=3$. Then $f(6)$ is equal to
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & \int_0^x t f(t) d t=x^2 f(x) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad x f(x)=2 x f(x)+x^2 f^{\prime}(x) \\ & \Rightarrow x^2 \cdot f^{\prime}(x)=-x f(x) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=-\frac{1}{x} \\ & \\ & \quad \int \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x) d x}=-\int \frac{1}{x} d x \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \ln f(x)=-\ln x+C \\ & \\ & \quad f(2)=3 \Rightarrow \ln 3=-\ln 2+C \\ & \quad C=\ln 6 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad f(x)=\frac{6}{x} \Rightarrow f(6)=1\end{aligned}$

question_text: Let $f(x)=\int_0^{x^2} \frac{\mathrm{t}^2-8 \mathrm{t}+15}{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{t}}} \mathrm{dt}, x \in \mathbf{R}$. Then the numbers of local maximum and local minimum points of $f$, respectively, are :
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned} & f(x)=\int_0^{x^2} \frac{t^2-8 t+15}{e^t} d t, x \in R \\ & f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{x^4-8 x^2+15}{e^{x^2}}(2 x)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{2 \times\left(x^2-5\right)\left(x^2-3\right)}{e^{x^2}}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow x(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5})(x+\sqrt{3})(x-\sqrt{3})=0 \end{aligned}$ By using wavy curve method
Number of local maximum $=2$ Number of local minimum $=3$

question_text: Let $\int_0^x \sqrt{1-\left(y^{\prime}(t)\right)^2} d t=\int_0^x y(t) d t, 0 \leq x \leq 3, y \geq 0, y(0)=0$. Then at $x=2, y^{\prime \prime}+y+1$ is equal to
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned} & \sqrt{1-\left(y^{\prime}(x)\right)^2}=y(x) \\ & 1-\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2=y^2 \\ & \left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2=1-y^2\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}=d x \text { OR } \frac{d y}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}=-d x \\ & \Rightarrow \sin ^{-1} y=x+c, \sin ^{-1} y=-x+c \\ & x=0, y=0 \Rightarrow c=0 \\ & \sin ^{-1} y=x, \text { as } y \geq 0 \\ & \sin x=y \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\cos x \\ & \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-\sin x \\ & \Rightarrow-\sin x+\sin x+1=1\end{aligned}$

question_text: The minimum value of the twice differentiable function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mfenced><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>x</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>'</mo></msup><mfenced><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>-</mo><mfenced><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi></math>, is

question_text: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi></math> be a twice differentiable function on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math>. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>'</mo></msup><mfenced><mn>0</mn></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mfenced><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mfenced><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>'</mo></msup><mfenced><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></math> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>=</mo><mfenced><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mfrac><mi>x</mi></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mfenced><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mn>5</mn></msup><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> is equal to _______.
solution_text:
Given,

fx+∫0xx-tf'tdt=e2x+e-2xcos2x+2xa     ⋯i

Putting x=0 both side we get, f0=2     ⋯ii

On differentiating equation i w.r.t. x we get:

f'x+∫0xf'tdt+xf'x-xf'x=2e2x-e-2xcos2x-2e2x+e-2xsin2x+2a

⇒f'x+fx-f0=2e2x-e-2xcos2x-2e2x+e-2xsin2x+2a

question_text: If $\alpha = \displaystyle\int_0^{2\sqrt{3}} \log_2(x^2 + 4)\,dx + \displaystyle\int_2^4 \sqrt{2^x - 4}\,dx$, then $\alpha^2$ is equal to _______.
solution_text:
Let $f(x) = \log_2(x^2 + 4)$ for $x \ge 0$.

To find the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$, we set $y = \log_2(x^2 + 4)$ and solve for $x$:

$2^y = x^2 + 4$

$x^2 = 2^y - 4$

$x = \sqrt{2^y - 4}$

Thus, $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{2^x - 4}$.

The given expression is $\alpha = \displaystyle\int_0^{2\sqrt{3}} f(x)\,dx + \displaystyle\int_2^4 f^{-1}(x)\,dx$.

We observe the limits of the first integral and evaluate the function at these points:

$f(0) = \log_2(0 + 4) = 2$

$f(2\sqrt{3}) = \log_2((2\sqrt{3})^2 + 4) = \log_2(12 + 4) = \log_2(16) = 4$

These exactly match the limits of the second integral. Using the standard property of definite integrals for inverse functions:

$\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \displaystyle\int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} f^{-1}(x)\,dx = b f(b) - a f(a)$

Substituting $a = 0$ and $b = 2\sqrt{3}$:

$\alpha = 2\sqrt{3} \cdot f(2\sqrt{3}) - 0 \cdot f(0)$

$\alpha = 2\sqrt{3} \cdot 4 - 0 = 8\sqrt{3}$

Therefore, $\alpha^2 = (8\sqrt{3})^2 = 64 \times 3 = 192$.

Answer: $192$

question_text: The value of the integral $\int\limits_{-1}^{1} \left(\dfrac{x^3 + |x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}\right) dx$ is equal to :
solution_text:
Let $I = \int_{-1}^{1} \left(\dfrac{x^3 + |x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}\right) dx$

We can split the integral into two parts:

$I = \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1} dx + \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{|x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1} dx$

The first integrand $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}$ is an odd function since $f(-x) = -f(x)$. Therefore, its integral over the symmetric interval $[-1, 1]$ is zero.

The second integrand $g(x) = \dfrac{|x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}$ is an even function since $g(-x) = g(x)$. Therefore, its integral over $[-1, 1]$ is twice the integral over $[0, 1]$.

$I = 0 + 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x + 1}{x^2 + 2x + 1} dx$

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x + 1}{(x + 1)^2} dx$

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x + 1} dx$

$I = 2 [\log_e(x + 1)]_{0}^{1}$

$I = 2(\log_e 2 - \log_e 1) = 2\log_e 2$

Answer: $2\log_e 2$

question_text: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ be a singular matrix. Let $f(x) = \int\limits_0^x (t^2 + 2t + 3)\,dt$, $x \in [1, \alpha]$. If $M$ and $m$ are respectively the maximum and the minimum values of $f$ in $[1, \alpha]$, then $3(M - m)$ is equal to :
solution_text:
Since $A$ is a singular matrix, $|A| = 0$.

$|A| = 1(-1 - \alpha) - 3(-2 - 0) - 1(2 - 0) = 0$

$-1 - \alpha + 6 - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = 3$

The function is $f(x) = \int\limits_0^x (t^2 + 2t + 3)\,dt = \dfrac{x^3}{3} + x^2 + 3x$

Differentiating with respect to $x$, we get $f'(x) = x^2 + 2x + 3 = (x+1)^2 + 2 > 0$ for all $x$.

Thus, $f(x)$ is a strictly increasing function on the interval $[1, 3]$.

The maximum value $M$ occurs at $x = 3$:

$M = f(3) = \dfrac{3^3}{3} + 3^2 + 3(3) = 9 + 9 + 9 = 27$

The minimum value $m$ occurs at $x = 1$:

$m = f(1) = \dfrac{1^3}{3} + 1^2 + 3(1) = \dfrac{13}{3}$

We need to find $3(M - m)$:

$3(M - m) = 3\left(27 - \dfrac{13}{3}\right) = 81 - 13 = 68$

Answer: $68$

question_text: The value of the integral $\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}}\right)dx$ is:
solution_text:
Let $I = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} dx$

Using the definite integral property $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) dx = \int_{0}^{a} (f(x) + f(-x)) dx$, we get:

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4(-x)}{1 + e^{\sin(-x)}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{-\sin x}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{32\cos^4 x}{1 + e^{\sin x}} + \dfrac{32\cos^4 x \cdot e^{\sin x}}{e^{\sin x} + 1} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 32\cos^4 x \left( \dfrac{1 + e^{\sin x}}{1 + e^{\sin x}} \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 32\cos^4 x dx$

Using the trigonometric identity $\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$, we can write:

$\cos^4 x = \left( \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} (1 + 2\cos 2x + \cos^2 2x)$

$\cos^4 x = \dfrac{1}{4} \left( 1 + 2\cos 2x + \dfrac{1 + \cos 4x}{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{8}\cos 4x$

Substituting this back into the integral:

$I = 32 \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{8}\cos 4x \right) dx$

$I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} (12 + 16\cos 2x + 4\cos 4x) dx$

Integrating term by term:

$I = \left[ 12x + 8\sin 2x + \sin 4x \right]_{0}^{\pi/4}$

$I = \left( 12\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \sin(\pi) \right) - (0 + 0 + 0)$

$I = 3\pi + 8(1) + 0 = 3\pi + 8$

Answer: $3\pi + 8$

question_text: Let $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} (|\sin x| + [x \sin x])\,dx = 2(3 - \cos 2) + \beta$, where $[\cdot]$ is the greatest integer function. Then $\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right)$ equals:
solution_text:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} \left(|\sin x| + [x \sin x]\right) dx = I_1 + I_2$, where
$I_1 = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} |\sin x|\, dx$ and $I_2 = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} [x \sin x]\, dx$.

Evaluating $I_1$:
Since $|\sin x|$ is even, $I_1 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} |\sin x|\, dx$.
For $x \in [0, 2]$, $2 < \pi$, so $\sin x \geq 0$ and $|\sin x| = \sin x$.
$I_1 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \sin x\, dx = 2\left[-\cos x\right]_0^2 = 2(1 - \cos 2) = 2 - 2\cos 2$

Evaluating $I_2$:
Let $g(x) = x\sin x$. Then $g(-x) = (-x)\sin(-x) = x\sin x = g(x)$, so $g(x)$ is even, and hence $[x\sin x]$ is also even.
$I_2 = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} [x\sin x]\, dx$

Behaviour of $y = x\sin x$ on $[0, 2]$:
At $x = 0$, $y = 0$. At $x = 2$, $y = 2\sin 2 \approx 1.818$.
$y' = \sin x + x\cos x > 0$ on $[0, 2]$, so $y$ is strictly increasing on this interval.

Therefore, $x\sin x$ takes each value in $[0, 1.818]$ exactly once, and crosses $1$ at some unique $\alpha \in (0, 2)$ with $\alpha\sin\alpha = 1$.

For $x \in [0, \alpha)$: $0 \leq x\sin x < 1 \Rightarrow [x\sin x] = 0$
For $x \in [\alpha, 2]$: $1 \leq x\sin x < 2 \Rightarrow [x\sin x] = 1$

$I_2 = 2\left(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\alpha} 0\, dx + \displaystyle\int_{\alpha}^{2} 1\, dx\right) = 2(2 - \alpha) = 4 - 2\alpha$

Combining:
$I = I_1 + I_2 = (2 - 2\cos 2) + (4 - 2\alpha) = 6 - 2\cos 2 - 2\alpha$

Given $I = 2(3 - \cos 2) + \beta = 6 - 2\cos 2 + \beta$, so:
$6 - 2\cos 2 - 2\alpha = 6 - 2\cos 2 + \beta \Rightarrow \beta = -2\alpha$

Now:
$\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right) = -2\alpha \sin\left(\dfrac{-2\alpha}{2}\right) = -2\alpha \sin(-\alpha) = 2\alpha\sin\alpha$

Since $\alpha\sin\alpha = 1$:
$\beta \sin\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2$

Hence, the correct option is $(2)\ 2$.

question_text: Let $[\cdot]$ denote the greatest integer function. Then the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^3 \left(\dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{[x]!}\right) dx$ is :
solution_text:
The given integral can be split at integer values of $x$ because of the greatest integer function $[x]$.

$\displaystyle I = \int_0^3 \left(\dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{[x]!}\right) dx$

$\displaystyle I = \int_0^1 \dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{0!} dx + \int_1^2 \dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{1!} dx + \int_2^3 \dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2!} dx$

Since $0! = 1$, $1! = 1$, and $2! = 2$, we get:

$\displaystyle I = \int_0^2 (e^x + e^{-x}) dx + \dfrac{1}{2} \int_2^3 (e^x + e^{-x}) dx$

Integrating the terms:

$\displaystyle I = \left[ e^x - e^{-x} \right]_0^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ e^x - e^{-x} \right]_2^3$

$\displaystyle I = (e^2 - e^{-2} - (1 - 1)) + \dfrac{1}{2} (e^3 - e^{-3} - (e^2 - e^{-2}))$

$\displaystyle I = e^2 - e^{-2} + \dfrac{1}{2} e^3 - \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-3} - \dfrac{1}{2} e^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-2}$

$\displaystyle I = \dfrac{1}{2} e^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} e^3 - \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-2} - \dfrac{1}{2} e^{-3}$

$\displaystyle I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( e^2 + e^3 - \dfrac{1}{e^2} - \dfrac{1}{e^3} \right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(e^2 + e^3 - \dfrac{1}{e^2} - \dfrac{1}{e^3}\right)$

question_text: Let $[\cdot]$ denote the greatest integer function. Then $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\frac{12(3+[x])}{3+[\sin x]+[\cos x]}\right) \mathrm{d} x$ is equal to :
The value of $\sum_{r=1}^{20}\left(\left|\sqrt{\pi\left(\int_{0}^{r} x|\sin \pi x| d x\right)}\right|\right)$ is $\_\_\_\_$
solution_text:
Let $I_r = \int_{0}^{r} x|\sin \pi x| \, dx$ .....(1)
Apply King Property
$= \int_{0}^{r} (r - x)|\sin \pi x| \, dx$ .....(2)
By (1) + (2)
$2I_r = \int_{0}^{r} r|\sin \pi x| \, dx \Rightarrow I_r = \dfrac{r}{2} \int_{0}^{r} |\sin \pi x| \, dx$
$I_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{1} |\sin \pi x| \, dx = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} |\sin t| \, dt = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}(2)$
$I_2 = \dfrac{2}{2} \int_{0}^{2} |\sin \pi x| \, dx = \dfrac{2}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} |\sin t| \, dt = \dfrac{2}{2\pi}(4)$
$S = \sqrt{\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \cdot 2} + \sqrt{\pi \cdot \dfrac{2}{2\pi} \cdot 4} + \sqrt{\pi \cdot \dfrac{3}{2\pi} \cdot 6} + \ldots + \sqrt{\pi \cdot \dfrac{20}{2\pi}(2 \cdot 20)}$
$= 1 + 2 + 3 + \ldots + 20$
$= \dfrac{20 \times 21}{2} = 210$

question_text: Let $f$ be a polynomial function such that $f\left(x^{2}+1\right)=x^{4}+5 x^{2}+2$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\int_{0}^{3} f(x) d x$ is equal to
solution_text:
Let $u = x^2 + 1$, then $x^2 = u - 1$.
Substituting into the given condition:
$f(u) = (u-1)^2 + 5(u-1) + 2 =$
$u^2 - 2u + 1 + 5u - 5 + 2$
$= u^2 + 3u - 2$.
Therefore, $f(x) = x^2 + 3x - 2$.
Calculating the integral: $\int_0^3 f(x)dx = \int_0^3 (x^2 + 3x - 2)dx$
$= \left[\frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{3x^2}{2} - 2x\right]_0^3 = 9 + \frac{27}{2} - 6 = \frac{33}{2}$.

question_text: The value of the integral $\int_{\frac{\pi}{24}}^{\frac{5 \pi}{24}} \frac{\mathrm{~d} x}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2 x}}$ is :
solution_text:
Let $I = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} \frac{dx}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}$.
Apply King's rule ($x \to \pi/4 - x$):
$I = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} \frac{dx}{1+\sqrt[3]{\cot 2x}} = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} \frac{\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}{1+\sqrt[3]{\tan 2x}}dx$.
Adding: $2I = \int_{\pi/24}^{5\pi/24} dx = \frac{5\pi}{24} - \frac{\pi}{24} = \frac{\pi}{6}$.
$I = \frac{\pi}{12}$.

question_text: Let $[\cdot]$ be the greatest integer function. If $\alpha=\int_{0}^{64}\left(x^{1 / 3}-\left[x^{1 / 3}\right]\right) \mathrm{d} x$, then $\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\alpha \pi}\left(\frac{\sin ^{2} \theta}{\sin ^{6} \theta+\cos ^{6} \theta}\right) \mathrm{d} \theta$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$ .
solution_text:
$\because \int_{0}^{64} x^{\frac{1}{3}} \, dx = \dfrac{3}{4} \left[ x^{\frac{4}{3}} \right]_{0}^{64} = 192$ &
$\int_{0}^{64} [x^{1/3}] \, dx = \int_{0}^{1} [x^{1/3}] \, dx + \int_{1}^{8} [x^{1/3}] \, dx + \int_{8}^{27} [x^{1/3}] \, dx + \int_{27}^{64} [x^{1/3}] \, dx = 156$
So $\alpha = 192 - 156 = 36$
Now $E = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{36\pi} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$
$= \dfrac{36}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$
$\Rightarrow E = \dfrac{36 \cdot 2}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$
Let $J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$ ....(1)
Applying King
$J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$ .....(2)
Now $2J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{1}{\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta} \, d\theta$ (add (1) & (2))
$= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sec^6\theta}{\tan^6\theta + 1} \, d\theta$
$= \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(1 + \lambda^2)}{\lambda^4 - \lambda^2 + 1} \, d\lambda$
$= \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}}{\lambda^2 - 1 + \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}} \, d\lambda$
$= \pi$
$\Rightarrow J = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
$\Rightarrow E = \dfrac{36 \cdot 2}{\pi} \times J = 36$

question_text: Let $f(x)=[x]^{2}-[x+3]-3, x \in \mathbf{R}$, where [] is the greatest integer funtion. Then
solution_text:
For $x \in [n, n+1)$ where $n$ is an integer, $[x] = n$ and $[x+3] = n+3$.
Thus $f(x) = n^2 - (n+3) - 3 = n^2 - n - 6 = (n-3)(n+2)$.
For $f(x) < 0$, we need $(n-3)(n+2) < 0$, which gives $-2 < n < 3$, i.e., $n \in \{-1, 0, 1, 2\}$.
This corresponds to $x \in [-1, 3)$.
We can verify:
For $n = -1$: $f = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4 < 0$
For $n = 0,1$: $f = -6 < 0$
For $n = 2$: $f = 4 - 5 - 3 = -4 < 0$
For $n = 3$: $f = 9 - 6 - 3 = 0$
For $n \geq 4$, $(n-3)(n+2) > 0$.
Therefore $f(x) < 0$ only for $x \in [-1, 3)$.

question_text: The value of $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\frac{1}{[x]+4}\right) d x$, where $[\cdot]$ denotes the greatest integer function, is
$6 \int_{0}^{\pi}|(\sin 3 x+\sin 2 x+\sin x)| d x$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
solution_text:
Using $\sin 3x + \sin x = 2\sin 2x \cos x$:
$\sin 3x + \sin 2x + \sin x = \sin 2x(2\cos x + 1) = 2\sin x \cos x(2\cos x + 1)$
Zeros in $[0, \pi]$: $x = 0, \pi/2, 2\pi/3, \pi$
Expression is positive on $(0, \pi/2)$, negative on $(\pi/2, 2\pi/3)$, positive on $(2\pi/3, \pi)$
Let $F(x) = -\frac{\cos 3x}{3} - \frac{\cos 2x}{2} - \cos x$
$F(0) = -\frac{11}{6}$, $F(\pi/2) = \frac{1}{2}$, $F(2\pi/3) = \frac{5}{12}$, $F(\pi) = \frac{5}{6}$
$\int_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{7}{3}$, $\left|\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}\right| = \frac{1}{12}$, $\int_{2\pi/3}^{\pi} = \frac{5}{12}$
Total $= \frac{7}{3} + \frac{1}{12} + \frac{5}{12} = \frac{17}{6}$
$6 \times \frac{17}{6} = 17$

question_text: The value of $\int_{-\pi / 6}^{\pi / 6}\left(\frac{\pi+4 x^{11}}{1-\sin (|x|+\pi / 6)}\right) d x$ is equal to:
solution_text:
Split: $\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{\pi}{1 - \sin(|x| + \pi/6)} dx + \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{4x^{11}}{1 - \sin(|x| + \pi/6)} dx$.
Second integral = 0 (odd function over symmetric interval).
First integral: $2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi/6} \frac{1}{1 - \sin(x + \pi/6)} dx$.
Let $u = x + \pi/6$: $= 2\pi \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \frac{1}{1 - \sin u} du$.
$\frac{1}{1-\sin u} = \sec^2 u + \sec u \tan u$.
$= 2\pi [\tan u + \sec u]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} = 2\pi[(\sqrt{3}+2) - \sqrt{3}] = 4\pi$.

question_text: The integral $\int_{-1}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\left|\pi^2 x \sin (\pi x)\right|\right) d x$ is equal to:
solution_text:
Let, $\mathrm{I}=\pi^2 \int_{-1}^{3 / 2}|\mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{x}| \mathrm{dx}$
$\begin{aligned}
& =\pi^2\left\{\int_{-1}^1 \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}-\int_1^{3 / 2} \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}\right\} \\ & =\pi^2\left\{2 \int_0^1 \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}-\int_{-1}^{3 / 2} \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx}\right\}
\end{aligned}$
Consider
$\begin{aligned}
& \int \mathrm{x} \sin \pi \mathrm{xdx} \\ & -\mathrm{x} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\int 1 \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{xdx} \\ & =-\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\frac{\sin \pi \mathrm{x}}{\pi^2}
\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{I} & =\pi^2\left\{2\left(-\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\frac{\sin \pi \mathrm{x}}{\pi^2}\right)_0^1-\left(-\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\pi} \cos \pi \mathrm{x}+\frac{\sin \pi \mathrm{x}}{\pi^2}\right)_1^{3 / 2}\right\} \\ & =\pi^2\left\{\frac{2}{\pi}-\left(-\frac{1}{\pi^2}-\frac{1}{\pi}\right)\right\} \\ & =\pi^2\left\{\frac{3}{\pi}+\frac{1}{\pi^2}\right\} \\ & =3 \pi+1\end{aligned}$

question_text: Let $f(x)$ be a positive function and $I_1=\int_{-\frac{1}{2}}^1 2 x f(2 x(1-2 x)) d x$ and $I_2=\int_{-1}^2 f(x(1-x)) d x$. Then the value of $\frac{I_2}{I_1}$ is equal to ________
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_1=\int_{-\frac{1}{2}}^1 2 \mathrm{xf}(2 \mathrm{x}(1-2 \mathrm{x})) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{t} \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{dt} \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_1=\frac{1}{2} \int_{-1}^2 \mathrm{tf}(\mathrm{t}(1-\mathrm{t})) \mathrm{dt} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}_1=\int_{-1}^2(1-\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{f}(1-\mathrm{t})(1-(1-\mathrm{t})) \mathrm{dt} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}_1=\int_{-1}^2 \mathrm{f}\left(\mathrm{t}(1-\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{dt}-\int_{-1}^2 \mathrm{tf}(\mathrm{t}(1-\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{dt}\right. \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}_1=\mathrm{I}_2-2 \mathrm{I}_1 \\ & \Rightarrow 4 \mathrm{I}_1=\mathrm{I}_2 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{I}_2}{\mathrm{I}_1}=4\end{aligned}$

question_text: The integral $\int_0^\pi \frac{(x+3) \sin x}{1+3 \cos ^2 x} d x$ is equal to :
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^\pi \frac{(x+3) \sin x}{1+3 \cos ^2 x} d x \\ & I=\int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-x+3) \sin x}{\left(1+3 \cos ^2 x\right)} d x \\ & 2 I=\int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi+6) \sin x \cdot d x}{\left(1+3 \cos ^2 x\right)}=2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{(\pi+6) \sin x}{\left(1+3 \cos ^2 x\right)} \\ & I=\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{(\pi+6) \sin x \cdot d x}{\left(1+3 \cos ^2 x\right)}=\frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{3}}(\pi+6) \\ & \sqrt{3} \cos x=t \\ & \sqrt{3} \sin x=d t\end{aligned}$

question_text: The value of $\int_{-1}^1 \frac{(1+\sqrt{|x|-x}) e^x+(\sqrt{|x|-x}) e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}} d x$ is equal to
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1 \frac{(1+\sqrt{|-\mathrm{x}|-(-\mathrm{x})}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}+(\sqrt{|-\mathrm{x}|-(-\mathrm{x})}) \mathrm{e}^{-(-\mathrm{x})}}{\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{-(-\mathrm{x})}} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1 \frac{(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}+(\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}}{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1 \frac{(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|-\mathrm{x}})\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}\right)}{\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{x}}\right)} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^1(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|-\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=2 \int_0^1(1+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|+\mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{|\mathrm{x}|-\mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=2 \int_0^1(1+\sqrt{2 \mathrm{x}}+\sqrt{0}) \mathrm{dx} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\int_0^1(1+\sqrt{2 \mathrm{x}}) \mathrm{dx}=\left[\mathrm{x}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} \mathrm{x}^{3 / 2}\right]_0^1 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}+1\end{aligned}$

question_text: The integral $\int_0^\pi \frac{8 x d x}{4 \cos ^2 x+\sin ^2 x}$ is equal to
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}
& I=\int_0^\pi \frac{8 x d x}{4 \cos ^2 x+\sin ^2 x} \\ & I=\int_0^\pi \frac{8(\pi-x) d x}{4 \cos ^2 x+\sin ^2 x}
\end{aligned}$
$2 \mathrm{I}=8 \pi \int_0^\pi \frac{d x}{4 \cos ^2 x+\sin ^2 x}$
$2 \mathrm{I}=8 \pi \times 2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\sec ^2 x}{4+\tan ^2 \mathrm{x}} \mathrm{dx}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{I}=8 \pi \int_0^{\infty} \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{4+\mathrm{t}^2}=8 \pi \times \frac{1}{2}\left(\tan ^{-1} \frac{\mathrm{t}}{2}\right]_0^{\infty} \\ & =4 \pi \times \frac{\pi}{2}=2 \pi^2
\end{aligned}$
option (1)

question_text:
Let the domain of the function
$f(\mathrm{x})=\log _2 \log _4 \log _6\left(3+4 x-x^2\right)$ be $(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{~b})$. If $\int_0^{\mathrm{b}-\mathrm{a}}\left[\mathrm{x}^2\right] \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{p}-\sqrt{\mathrm{q}}-\sqrt{\mathrm{r}}, \mathrm{p}, \mathrm{q},$ $\mathrm{r} \in \mathbb{N}, \operatorname{gcd}(\mathrm{p}, \mathrm{q}, \mathrm{r})=1,$
where [$\cdot]$ is the greatest integer function, then $\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}+\mathrm{r}$ is equal to
solution_text:

question_text: $4 \int_0^1\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3+x^2}+\sqrt{1+x^2}}\right) d x-3 \log _e(\sqrt{3})$ is equal to :
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned} & 4 \int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}+\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}} \mathrm{dx}-3 \ln \sqrt{3} \\ & =4 \int_0^1 \frac{\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}-\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}}{\left(3+\mathrm{x}^2\right)-\left(1-\mathrm{x}^2\right)} \mathrm{dx}-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & = \\ & 2\left[\left\{\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2} \sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}+\frac{3}{2} \ln \left(\mathrm{x}+\sqrt{3+\mathrm{x}^2}\right)\right\}_0^1\right. \\ & \left.\quad-\left\{\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2} \sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}+\frac{1}{2} \ln \left(\mathrm{x}+\sqrt{1+\mathrm{x}^2}\right)\right\}_0^1\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}= & 2\left[\left\{\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{4}+\frac{3}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{4})\right\}-\left\{0+\frac{3}{2} \ln \sqrt{3}\right\}\right. \\ & \left.-\left\{\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2}+\frac{1}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{2})\right\}+\left\{0+\frac{1}{2}(0)\right\}\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & =2\left[1+\frac{3}{2} \ln 3-\frac{3}{4} \ln 3-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{1}{2} \ln (1+\sqrt{2})\right]-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & =2+3 \ln 3-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3-\sqrt{2}-\ln (1+\sqrt{2})-\frac{3}{2} \ln 3 \\ & =2-\sqrt{2}-\ln (1+\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}$

question_text: Let $(a, b)$ be the point of intersection of the curve $x^2=2 y$ and the straight line $y-2 x-6=0$ in the second quadrant. Then the integral $I=\int_a^b \frac{9 x^2}{1+5^x} d x$ is equal to :
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned} & x^2=2 y \& y=2 x+6 \\ & x^2=4 x+12\end{aligned}$
$\left.x^2-4 x-12=0 \Rightarrow \begin{gathered}x=6 \\ y=18\end{gathered} \right\rvert\, \begin{gathered}\text { if } x=-2 \\ y=2\end{gathered}$
$\therefore(6,18) \&(-2,2)$
Here $(6,18)$ Rejected because $(a, b)$ lies in $2^{\text {nd }}$ quadrant
$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{a}=-2 \& \mathrm{~b}=2 \\ & \therefore \mathrm{I}=\int_{-2}^2 \frac{9 \mathrm{x}^2}{1+5^{\mathrm{x}}} \mathrm{dx}=\int_{-2}^2 \frac{9 \cdot 5^{\mathrm{x}} \cdot \mathrm{x}^2}{1+5^{\mathrm{x}}} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \therefore 2 \mathrm{I}=\int_{-2}^2 9 \mathrm{x}^2 \mathrm{dx}=18 \int_0^2 \mathrm{x}^2 \mathrm{dx}=18\left(\frac{\mathrm{x}^3}{3}\right)_0^2 \\ & 2 \mathrm{I}=48 \\ & \therefore \mathrm{I}=24\end{aligned}$

question_text: Let [.] denote the greatest integer function. If $\int_0^{e^3}\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}-1}}\right] \mathrm{dx}=\alpha-\log _{\mathrm{e}} 2$, then $\alpha^3$ is equal to _______ .
solution_text:
$f(x)=\frac{1}{e^{x-1}}=e^{1-x}$
\begin{array}{c|c}\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})=2 & \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})=1 \\\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}-1}}=2 & \mathrm{x}=1 \\\mathrm{x}=1-\ln 2 &\end{array}
$f(0)=e^1=2.71$
$f\left(e^3\right)=e^{1-e^3} \in(0,1)$
$\mathrm{I}=\int_0^{1-\ell \mathrm{n} 2} 2 \mathrm{dx}+\int_{1-\ell \mathrm{n} 2}^1 1 \mathrm{dx}+\int_1^{\mathrm{e}^3} 0 \mathrm{dx}$
$=2(1-\ell \operatorname{n} 2-0)+1(1-1+\ln 2)+0$
$\alpha-\ln 2=2-\ln 2$
$\alpha=2$
$\alpha^3=8$

question_text: If $24 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sin \left|4 x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right|+[2 \sin x]\right) \mathrm{d} x=2 \pi+\alpha$, where $[\cdot]$ denotes the greatest integer function, then $\alpha$ is equal to _______.
solution_text:
Let $I=24 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\sin \left|4 x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right|+[2 \sin x]\right) d x$   ...(i)
Now $\left|4 x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right|= \begin{cases}-4 x+\frac{\pi}{12} & ; x < \frac{\pi}{48} \\ 4 x-\frac{\pi}{12} & ; \quad x \geq \frac{\pi}{48}\end{cases}$
$\therefore$ from $(\mathrm{i})$
$\begin{aligned} & I=24 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{48}}-\sin \left(4 x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right) d x+\int_{\frac{\pi}{48}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sin \left(4 x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right) \\ & +\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}[2 \sin x] d x+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}[2 \sin x] d x \\ & I=24\left[\frac{\left(1-\cos \frac{\pi}{12}\right)}{4}-\frac{\left(-\cos \frac{\pi}{12}-1\right)}{4}\right)+\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & I=24\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & I=2 \pi+12=2 \pi+\alpha \text { (from above) } \\ & \therefore \quad \alpha=12\end{aligned}$

question_text: If $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{96 x^2 \cos ^2 x}{\left(1+e^x\right)} \mathrm{d} x=\pi\left(\alpha \pi^2+\beta\right), \alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{Z}$, then $(\alpha+\beta)^2$ equals
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{96 x^2 \cos ^2 x}{1+e^x} d x \\ & 2 I=2 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 96 x^2 \cos ^2 x d x \\ & I=96 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^2 \cos ^2 x d x \\ & =48 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^2(1+\cos 2 x) d x \\ & =2 \pi^2+48(0-0)-48 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x \sin 2 x d x \\ & =2 \pi^2-12 \pi+[0-0]=\pi\left(2 \pi^2-12\right) \\ & =\pi\left(\alpha \pi^2+\beta\right) \\ & \Rightarrow(\alpha+\beta)^2=100\end{aligned}$

question_text: If $\mathrm{I}=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\sin ^{\frac{3}{2}} x}{\sin ^{\frac{3}{2}} x+\cos ^{\frac{3}{2}} x} \mathrm{~d} x$, then $\int_0^{21} \frac{x \sin x \cos x}{\sin ^4 x+\cos ^4 x} \mathrm{~d} x$ equals :
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}
& I=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}} d x}{(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}} x+(\cos x)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\sin ^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) d x}{\sin ^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)+\cos ^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)} \\
& \Rightarrow \text { Adding } 2 l=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}}+(\cos x)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}}+(\cos x)^{\frac{3}{2}}} d x=\frac{\pi}{2} \\
& I_0=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{x \sin x \cos x}{\sin ^4 x+\cos ^4 x} d x=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) \sin x \cos x}{(\sin x)^4+(\cos x)^4} d x
\end{aligned}$
Adding, $2 I_0=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\frac{\pi}{2}(\sin x) \cos x}{\left(\sin ^4 x+\cos ^4 x\right)} d x$
$\Rightarrow I_0=\frac{\pi}{4} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\tan x\left(\sec ^2 x\right) d x}{1+\tan ^4 x}$
put $\tan ^2 x=t \Rightarrow 2 \tan x \sec ^2 x d x=d t$
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow I_0=\frac{\pi}{4} \int_0^{\infty} \frac{\frac{d t}{2}}{\left(1+t^2\right)}=\left.\frac{\pi}{8}\left(\tan ^{-1} t\right)\right|_0 ^{\infty}=\frac{\pi}{8}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-0\right) \\
& \Rightarrow I_0=\frac{\pi^2}{16}
\end{aligned}$

question_text:
The value of
$\int_{e^2}^{e^4} \frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{e^{\left(\left(\log _e x\right)^2+1\right)^{-1}}}{e^{\left(\left(\log _e x\right)^2+1\right)^{-1}}+e^{\left(\left(6-\log _e x\right)^2+1\right)^{-1}}}\right) d x$ is

\hline x & t \\

& I=\int_2^4 \frac{e^{\left((6-t)^2+1\right)^{-1}}}{e^{\left((6-t)^2+1\right)^{-1}}+e^{\left(t^2+1\right)^{-1}} d t} \ldots \text { (ii) } \\

Adding (i) and (ii) gives
$2 l=\int d t \Rightarrow l=1$

question_text: The value of the integral $\int_{-1}^2 \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right) d x$ is
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned} & I=\int_{-1}^2 \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right) d x \\ & =x \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)-\int_{-1}^2\left(\frac{1+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}}\right) d x \\ & =x \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)-\int_{-1}^2 \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} d x\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & =x \log _e\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)-\left.\sqrt{x^2+1}\right|_{-1} ^2 \\ & =\left(2 \log _e(2+\sqrt{5})-\sqrt{5}\right) \\ & -\left(-\log _e(-1+\sqrt{2})-\sqrt{2}\right) \\ & =\log _e(2+\sqrt{5})^2-\sqrt{5}+\log _e(\sqrt{2}-1)+\sqrt{2} \\ & =\log _e(2+\sqrt{5})^2-\sqrt{5}+\log _e(\sqrt{2}-1)+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & =\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{5}+\log _e\left(\frac{(2+\sqrt{5})^2}{\sqrt{2+1}}\right) \\ & =\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{5}+\log _e\left(\frac{9+4 \sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{2+1}}\right)\end{aligned}$

question_text: If $f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{2 x \mathrm{~d} x}{1-\cos ^2 \mathrm{t} \sin ^2 x}, 0 < \mathrm{t} < \pi$, then the value of $\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\pi^2 \mathrm{dt}}{f(\mathrm{t})}$ equals_________
solution_text:
$f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{2 x}{1-\cos ^2 t \sin ^2 x} d x$ .....(1)
$=2 \int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-x) d x}{1-\cos ^2 \sin ^2 x}$ .....(2)
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 f(t)=2 \int_0^\pi \frac{\pi}{1-\cos ^2 \sin ^2 x} d x \\
& f(t)=\int_0^\pi \frac{\pi}{1-\cos ^2 t \sin ^2 x} d x
\end{aligned}$
divide \& by $\cos ^2 \mathrm{x}$
$\begin{aligned}
& f(t)=\pi \int_0^\pi \frac{\sec ^2 x d x}{\sec ^2 x-\cos ^2 t^2 x} \\
& f(t)=2 \pi \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\sec ^2 x d x}{\sec ^2 x-\cos ^2 t^2 \tan ^2 x} \\
& \tan x=z \\
& \sec ^2 x d x=d z \\
& f(t)=2 \pi \int_0^{\infty} \frac{d z}{1+\sin ^2 t \cdot z^2} \\
& =\frac{\pi^2}{\sin t}
\end{aligned}$
Then $\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\pi^2}{f(t)} d t$
$\begin{aligned}
& =\int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin t d t \\
& =1
\end{aligned}$

question_text: The integral $\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{136 \sin x}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x} d x$ is equal to :
solution_text:
$\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{136 \sin x}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x} d x \\ & 136 \sin x=A(3 \sin x+5 \cos x)+B(3 \cos x-5 \sin x) \\ & 136=3 A-5 B...(i) \\ & 0=5 A+3 B...(ii)\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & 3 \mathrm{~B}=-5 \mathrm{~A} \Rightarrow \mathrm{B}=-\frac{5}{3} \mathrm{~A} \\ & 136=3 \mathrm{~A}-5\left(-\frac{5}{3} \mathrm{~A}\right) \\ & 136=3 \mathrm{~A}+\frac{25}{3} \mathrm{~A} \\ & 136=\frac{34 \mathrm{~A}}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{A}=\frac{136 \times 3}{34}=12 \\ & \mathrm{~B}=\frac{-5}{3}(12)=-20\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{A(3 \sin x+5 \cos x)}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x}+\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{B(3 \cos x-5 \sin x)}{3 \sin x+5 \cos x} \\ & =A(x)_0^{\pi / 4}+B[\ln (3 \sin x+5 \cos x)]_0^{\pi / 4} \\ & =12\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-20 \ln \left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\right)-\ln (0+5) \\ & =3 \pi-20 \ln 4 \sqrt{2}+20 \ln 5 \\ & =3 \pi-20 \times \frac{5}{2} \ln 2+20 \ln 5 \\ & =3 \pi-50 \ln 2+20 \ln 5\end{aligned}$

question_text: The value of $\int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{2 y(1+\sin y)}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y$ is :
solution_text:
$\int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{2 y(1+\sin y)}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y$ \(=\underset{\text{(Odd)}}{\int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{2 y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y}+\underset{\text{(Even)}}{\int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{2 y \sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y}\)
$=0+2.2 \int_0^\pi y\left(\frac{\sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y}\right) d y$ $\begin{aligned} & I=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{y \sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & I=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-y) \sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & 2 I=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{\pi \sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & I=2 \pi \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin y}{1+\cos ^2 y} d y \\ & =2 \pi\left(-\tan ^{-1}(\cos y)\right)_0^\pi \\ & =-2 \pi\left[\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right] \\ & =-2 \pi\left[-\frac{2 \pi}{4}\right]=\pi^2\end{aligned}$

question_text: If the value of the integral $\int_{-1}^1 \frac{\cos \alpha x}{1+3^x} d x$ is $\frac{2}{\pi}$. Then, a value of $\alpha$ is
solution_text:
Let $I=\int_{-1}^{+1} \frac{\cos \alpha x}{1+3^x} d x$ ...(I)
$I=\int_{-1}^{+1} \frac{\cos \alpha x}{1+3^{-x}} d x$
$\left(u \operatorname{sing} \int_a^b f(x) d x=\int_a^b f(a+b-x) d x\right)$ ...(II)
Add (1) and (II)
$\begin{aligned}

& I=\frac{\sin \alpha}{\alpha}=\frac{2}{\pi}(\text { given }) \\
& \therefore \alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}
\end{aligned}$

question_text: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced close="|" open="|"><mrow><mfrac><mn>120</mn><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><munderover><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>π</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>sin</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>cos</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> is equal to ______.
solution_text:

The value of the integral $\int_{-2}^{2} \frac{\sin ^{2} x}{\left[\frac{x}{\pi}\right]+\frac{1}{2}} d x$

(where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to x) is
solution_text:
Let $f(x)=\frac{\sin ^{2} x}{\left[\frac{x}{\pi}\right]+\frac{1}{2}}$.

$\begin{array}{l}

\text { So, } f(-x)=\frac{\sin ^{2}(-x)}{\left[\frac{-x}{\pi}\right]+\frac{1}{2}} \quad \because[-x]=-1-[x] \\

\Rightarrow f(-x)=\frac{\sin ^{2} x}{-1-\left[\frac{x}{\pi}\right]+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{\sin ^{2} x}{-\frac{1}{2}-\left[\frac{x}{\pi}\right]}=-f(x)

\end{array}$

$\Rightarrow f(x)$ is odd function

Hence, $\int_{-2}^{2} f(x) d x=0$

question_text: If [ ] denotes the greatest integer function, then the integral $\int_0^\pi[\cos x d x$ is equal to:
solution_text:
Let $\mathrm{I}=\int_0^\pi[\cos x] d x$
$$
\mathrm{I}=\int_0^\pi[\cos (\pi-x)] d x=\int_0^\pi[-\cos x] d x
$$
On adding (1) and (2), we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
&2 \mathrm{I}=\int_0^\pi[\cos x] d x+\int_0^\pi[-\cos x] d x \\
&2 \mathrm{I}=\int_0^\pi[\cos x]+[-\cos x] d x \\
&2 \mathrm{I} \\
&=\int_0^\pi-1 d x \quad(\because[x]+[-x]=-1 \text { if } x \notin Z) \\
&2 \mathrm{I}=-\left.x\right|_0 ^\pi=-\pi \\
&\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\frac{-\pi}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

question_text: If $[x]$ is the greatest integer $\leq x$, then the value of the integral $\int_{-0.9}^{0.9}\left(\left[x^2\right]+\log \left(\frac{2-x}{2+x}\right)\right) d x$ is
solution_text:
$$
\text { } \begin{aligned}
& \int_{-0.9}^{0.9}\left\{\left[x^2\right]+\log \left(\frac{2-x}{2+x}\right)\right\} d x \\
= & \int_{-0.9}^{0.9}\left[x^2\right] d x+\int_{-0.9}^{0.9} \log \left(\frac{2-x}{2+x}\right) d x
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =0+\int_{-0.9}^{0.9} \log \left(\frac{2-x}{2+x}\right) d x \\
& \text { Put } x=-x \Rightarrow f(x)=\log \frac{2-x}{2+x} \\
& \text { and } f(-x)=\log \frac{2+x}{2-x} \\
& =-\log \frac{(2-x)}{2+x}=-f(x)
\end{aligned}
$$
So, it is an odd function, hence Required integral $=0$.

question_text: The value of $\int_0^{20\pi} (\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x) \, dx$ is equal to:
solution_text:
Let $I = \int_0^{20\pi} (\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x) \, dx$

Using the algebraic identity $a^2 + b^2 = (a+b)^2 - 2ab$, the integrand can be simplified:

$\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x = (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x)^2 - 2\sin^2 x \cos^2 x$

Since $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ and $2\sin x \cos x = \sin 2x$:

$\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} (2\sin x \cos x)^2 = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \sin^2 2x$

Using the half-angle formula $\sin^2 \theta = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}$:

$\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{1 - \cos 4x}{2} \right) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \cos 4x = \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \cos 4x$

Substituting this back into the integral:

$I = \int_0^{20\pi} \left( \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \cos 4x \right) \, dx$

$I = \left[ \dfrac{3}{4} x + \dfrac{1}{16} \sin 4x \right]_0^{20\pi}$

Evaluating the limits:

$I = \left( \dfrac{3}{4} (20\pi) + \dfrac{1}{16} \sin(80\pi) \right) - (0 + 0)$

Since $\sin(80\pi) = 0$:

$I = 15\pi$

Answer: $15\pi$

question_text: $\operatorname{IfI}(m, n)=\int_0^1 x^{m-1}(1-x)^{n-1} d x, m, n\gt0$, then $I(9,14)+I(10,13)$ is
solution_text: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}(\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{m})=\int_0^1 \mathrm{x}^{\mathrm{m}-1}(1-\mathrm{x})^{\mathrm{n}-1} d \mathrm{x} \\ & \text { Let } \mathrm{x}=\sin ^2 \theta \quad \mathrm{dx}=2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \mathrm{~d} \theta \\ & \mathrm{I}(\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{n})=2 \int_0^{\pi / 2}(\sin \theta)^{2 \mathrm{~m}-1}(\cos \theta)^{2 \mathrm{n}-1} d \theta \\ & \mathrm{I}(9,14)+\mathrm{I}(10,13)=2 \int_0^{\pi / 2}(\sin \theta)^{17}(\cos \theta)^{27} d \theta \\ & +2 \int_0^{\pi / 2}(\sin \theta)^{19}(\cos \theta)^{25} d \theta \\ & =2 \int_0^{\pi / 2}(\sin \theta)^{17}(\cos \theta)^{25} d \theta \\ & =\mathrm{I}(9,13)\end{aligned}$
